claims.text: The baseline synthesis produces PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts with a broad nanoparticle-size distribution.
A broad nanoparticle-size distribution creates heterogeneous active sites with mixed coordination environments.
The baseline catalysts have a lower proportion of low-coordination active sites than the proposed modified catalysts.
Surfactant-assisted wet-chemical reduction can produce a smaller and narrower nanoparticle-size distribution than the baseline synthesis.
Thermal annealing in an inert atmosphere or solvent washing can rigorously remove surfactant residues and eliminate ligand effects.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume atom ratio.
Reducing nanoparticle size increases the proportion of low-coordination surface atoms.
Low-coordination sites on PtPdRhRuIrOs have modified adsorption characteristics for ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
Modified adsorption at low-coordination sites changes the ethanol-oxidation reaction pathway.
The pathway change favors more complete ethanol oxidation and increases CO2 formation.
Increasing the density of low-coordination sites enhances ethanol-oxidation activity.
The surfactant-assisted and cleaned catalysts will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in ethanol-oxidation onset potential.
The surfactant-assisted and cleaned catalysts will exhibit higher ethanol-oxidation current density.
The surfactant-assisted and cleaned catalysts will exhibit a product distribution distinct from that of the baseline catalysts.
The proposed size-dependent mechanism applies to PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles from below 10 nm to approximately 20 nm.
The proposed mechanism applies under ambient-temperature electrochemical ethanol-oxidation conditions using standard electrolyte concentrations and applied potentials.
Failure of the intervention to produce a statistically significant nanoparticle-size difference would falsify the proposed low-coordination-site mechanism.
Absence of improvement in onset potential or current density, or absence of a measurable product-distribution change, would falsify the hypothesis.
